newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Traub attracts takeover interest.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Traub attracts takeover interest.

text.p: German toolmaker Traub AG's chances of surviving its insolvency crisis seemed brighter on Thursday as the company's court-appointed administrator said two companies were keen to take it over.

Volker Grub told a news conference that German toolmaking firm Gildemeister and a large U.S. toolmaker had expressed serious interest in acquiring Traub, which entered crisis talks with its creditors earlier this month.
Grub also said another company had signed a letter of intent to take over one of Traub's units, Heckert Chemnitzer Werkzeugmaschinen.
"It all looks very, very positive," Grub said.

After years in the red and having failed to find an international partner, Traub declared itself insolvent on October 15 and started so-called composition proceedings -- the German legal system's last defence against bankruptcy.
The threatened crisis was the latest in a series to hit the medium-sized firms -- known as 'Mittelstand' -- which form the backbone of Germany's economy.
On Thursday, Grub said Traub's founding Traub-van-Kempen family was willing to part with its 27 percent stake in the company. The remaining shares were broadly distributed.
He added that Traub's 14 creditor banks had declared themselves willing to co-operate in a restructuring of the company's finances.
The banks are owed a total of 230 million marks ($152 million) and it remains unclear how much of that repayment they may be willing to forgo.

Grub also said he was confident that Traub would be able to repay a required quota of 35 percent of the total 120 million marks owed to its 400 regular creditors, who will take part in court-based composition proceedings.
In order to survive the process, Traub would need a cut in its capital in the ratio of one to four followed by a capital increase of 50 million marks, Grub proposed.
Traub's stock has plunged amid revelations of its difficulties and closed bourse dealings at 18 marks on Thursday, off a year-high of 145 marks.
Grub added that Traub planned to cut more than 100 jobs in its headquarters in Reichenbach, south-west Germany.
Around 1,100 of Traub's 2,300 staff agreed last March to accept an eight percent wage cut for five months as the company struggled to survive.
German machine toolmakers, with the exception of isolated specialist firms, have been under mounting pressure for years.
Deckel Maho AG, one of the leading names in the industry, was rescued from the brink of collapse in mid-1994 when it was taken over by Gildemeister.
Gildemeister itself has since undergone a broad restructuring. It remains loss-making, although it reduced its net loss in 1995 to 22.9 million marks from 41.1 million marks the previous year.
